terms.meaning: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Position in the range shows where today's price sits between the two.
Absolute return is the total change over the whole period. Annualised return converts it to a yearly rate.
Money the company owes its suppliers for goods and services it has received but not yet paid for.
Money customers owe the company for goods or services already delivered.
Past prices, EPS and dividends recalculated as if today's share count had always applied, after splits and bonuses.
A message FinLit sends when a condition you set comes true, such as a price target, a big move, a score change or a results announcement.
The highest price a share has ever closed at, adjusted for splits and bonuses.
terms.formula: Distance from high % = (Price ÷ All-time high − 1) × 100

terms.meaning: A score combining five ratios to estimate the risk of bankruptcy within two years. It was designed for manufacturing companies.
The Association of Mutual Funds in India, the industry body whose public files publish every scheme's daily NAV.
aliases: Association of Mutual Funds in India

terms.meaning: Spreading a cost over time. For intangible assets such as software or licences, it works like depreciation. For loans, it means repaying in instalments, each covering interest and part of the principal.
A large institution that commits to buy part of the QIB portion one working day before the IPO opens, applying for at least ₹10 crore.
The yearly cost of a loan including interest and compulsory fees, as a percentage.
terms.formula: APR = ((Interest + Fees) ÷ Principal) ÷ Days in term × 365 × 100

terms.meaning: The yearly document every listed company publishes, with audited financial statements, the management discussion, the auditor's report and governance details.
A hybrid fund that buys shares in the cash market and sells the same shares in the futures market at the same time, earning the small price gap between the two.
The system that blocks your application money in your bank account instead of debiting it. Money is taken only if you get shares.
Anything a company owns that has value and can bring future benefit, such as cash, factories, inventory or money owed by customers.
terms.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Equity

terms.meaning: How your money is split between asset classes such as shares, bonds, gold and cash.
Revenue divided by average total assets: how many rupees of sales each rupee of assets produces.
terms.formula: Asset turnover = Revenue ÷ Average total assets

terms.meaning: The total market value of the money a fund holds for its investors, usually in rupees crore.
The yardstick on FinLit's Rotation page: every NSE industry and sector group with a reading, each counted equally.
The average size of a day's full price range, including any gap from the previous close, usually over 14 days. It is in rupees, not percent.
terms.formula: True range = Largest of (High − Low, |High − Previous close|, |Low − Previous close|); ATR = Average of true range

terms.meaning: Average volume is the typical daily volume over a window such as 20 days. A spike is a day far above that average.
A snapshot of what a company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and what belongs to shareholders (equity) on one date.
terms.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity

terms.meaning: The growth in loans given by banks, usually against the same date a year earlier.
A base is a period when the price moves sideways in a range after a rise or a fall. A breakout is a close above the top of that range.
When a growth rate looks unusually high or low because the starting figure was unusually low or high.
Earnings per share using only the shares that exist today: profit left for ordinary shareholders divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares.
terms.formula: Basic EPS = (Net profit − Preference dividends) ÷ Weighted average ordinary shares

terms.meaning: The final decision on who gets how many shares, published by the registrar after the issue closes.
A saved query from FinLit's Query builder. FinLit shows how many listed companies each basket matches today.
A standard you measure performance against, usually an index such as the Nifty 50 or Nifty 500.
How much a stock tends to move when the market moves. A beta of 1 moves with the market; 1.5 moves about 50% more; 0.5 about half as much.
Your application in an IPO: how many lots and at what price within the band.
A large, well-established company with a long record of steady profits, such as the biggest Nifty 50 names.
A meeting of the company's board of directors, which must be announced in advance when it will approve results, dividends or fund raising.
A loan you give to a government or company in return for regular interest and repayment of the amount on a set date.
Free extra shares given to existing shareholders in a fixed ratio, such as 1:1 (one new share for each share held).
The method most IPOs use to set the price: investors bid within a price band and the final price is decided from the demand.
The value of a company, or of an asset, as recorded in the accounts: assets minus liabilities for a company, cost minus depreciation for an asset.
terms.formula: Book value = Total assets − Total liabilities

terms.meaning: Shareholders' equity divided by the number of shares.
terms.formula: Book value per share = Shareholders' equity ÷ Shares outstanding

terms.meaning: All loans, bonds and debentures the company has taken, short and long term.

A sudden, broad rebound in an industry after a washout: in a few sessions most of its stocks turn up together. A CAP thrust is one that comes after a capitulation, a sell-off in which almost every stock kept falling to the end.
The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so the company makes neither profit nor loss.
terms.formula: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price − Variable cost per unit)

terms.meaning: Indices that cover a wide slice of the market by size: the Nifty 500 holds the 500 largest companies, the Nifty Midcap 150 the 150 after the top 100, and the Nifty Smallcap 250 the 250 after those.
A broker is a SEBI-registered firm that places your buy and sell orders on the exchange. The trading account is the account you use with them to place orders; it is linked to your demat account.

terms.term: Build-up (long build-up, short build-up, short covering, long unwinding)
terms.meaning: Labels that combine the day's price change with the change in open interest: long build-up (price up, OI up), short build-up (price down, OI up), short covering (price up, OI down) and long unwinding (price down, OI down).
A bull market is a long stretch of rising prices; a bear market is a long stretch of falling prices, often defined as a fall of 20% or more from a peak.
The group FinLit puts a company in before it reads cash-flow warnings: General, Capital-intensive, Project and EPC, Seasonal, or Trading and distribution.
When a company buys its own shares from shareholders, usually at a premium to the market price, and cancels them.
The steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting level to its ending level over several years.
terms.formula: CAGR = (Ending value ÷ Beginning value)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
aliases: Book value growth, 5 years a year

terms.meaning: The return from 1 January to 31 December of one year.
A chart symbol showing a day's open, high, low and close. A green candle closed above its open; a red one closed below.

Shapes of one to three daily candles that chart readers give names to, such as a hammer (a long lower wick after a fall), a bullish engulfing candle (an up candle that covers the previous down candle) or an upper-wick rejection (a long upper wick, where the day's highs did not hold).

terms.term: Capex intensity (capex to sales, capex to operating cash)
terms.meaning: Capital spending as a share of revenue or of operating cash flow.
aliases: capex to sales, capex to operating cash

terms.meaning: A bank's capital as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets.
Money spent on long-term assets such as factories, machines, stores or networks.
The profit from selling an asset for more than you paid for it. A capital loss is the opposite.
terms.formula: Capital gain = Sale price − Purchase price

terms.meaning: Tax on profit from selling investments. For listed shares and equity funds, gains on holdings of up to 12 months are short-term (STCG); longer are long-term (LTCG).
A capitulation is a sell-off in which almost every stock of an industry kept making new lows right up to the industry's low, instead of turning up one by one before it.
A single statement, from CAMS and KFintech or from the depositories (NSDL and CDSL), that lists all your mutual fund holdings across fund houses, with transactions.
Current-account and savings-account deposits as a share of a bank's total deposits.
Money in the bank and very short-term, very safe investments that can be turned into cash at once.
Operating cash flow as a percentage of net profit. FinLit also shows free cash flow to profit.
terms.formula: Cash conversion % = Operating cash flow ÷ Net profit × 100

terms.meaning: The number of days between paying for materials and collecting cash from customers.
terms.formula: Cash conversion cycle = Inventory days + Debtor days − Payable days

terms.meaning: The report of cash that actually came in and went out, split into operating, investing and financing activities.

terms.term: Category median and rank in category
terms.meaning: The category median is the middle figure among funds in the same SEBI category: half did better and half worse. Rank in category orders the category's funds on one measure, such as 3-year return.
The maximum a stock's price may rise or fall in one day, set by the exchange (for example 5%, 10% or 20%). A stock 'hits the upper circuit' when it reaches that limit.
The standard deviation divided by the average. It makes variability comparable across measures of different size.
terms.formula: Coefficient of variation = Standard deviation ÷ Mean

terms.meaning: Raw materials traded in bulk, such as gold, silver, crude oil and copper.
A profit and loss statement shown as a share of revenue, or a balance sheet as a share of total assets, so every line reads per ₹100.
terms.formula: Line as % of revenue = Line ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.term: Company size bands (mega cap to nano cap)
terms.meaning: Size groups based on a company's market value, from the very largest (mega cap) to the very smallest (micro and nano cap).
Interest earned on both your original money and the interest it has already earned.
How much of a portfolio sits in a few stocks or sectors.
A company that runs several unrelated businesses, such as energy, retail and telecom.
How regularly a company grows, for example 'profit rose in 4 of the last 5 years' or 'sales rose year on year in each of the last 4 quarters'.
aliases: Quarters of rising profit (last 4, year on year)
Quarters of rising sales (last 4, year on year)

terms.meaning: Standalone results cover only the listed company itself. Consolidated results add up the parent and all its subsidiaries, as if they were one business.
Any company decision that changes its shares or what shareholders receive: dividends, bonuses, splits, buybacks, rights issues, mergers and demergers.
aliases: Corporate actions in the last year

terms.meaning: A number from −1 to +1 that shows how closely two measures move together. +1 means they always move in step, −1 means always in opposite directions, and 0 means no straight-line link. Pearson's r uses the values themselves; Spearman's rho uses their ranks, so a few extreme points matter less.
terms.formula: r = Covariance(X, Y) ÷ (Standard deviation of X × Standard deviation of Y)

terms.meaning: How much less a regular investment grows to if it starts later and stops on the same date.
The stocks of an NSE industry that pass FinLit's counting rules, and so enter its breadth readings and its equal-weighted industry index.
How much of the information a FinLit Prism rating needs was actually found in the company's filings and prices, from 0% to 100%. A short sales and profit record counts only in part.
terms.formula: Coverage = 0.40 × Growth & Profitability coverage + 0.30 × Valuation coverage + 0.20 × Quality coverage + 0.10 × Risk coverage

terms.term: CPI and WPI (consumer and wholesale price indices)
terms.meaning: The consumer price index (CPI) tracks the prices households pay for a basket of goods and services; the wholesale price index (WPI) tracks prices at the wholesale level. Inflation is usually quoted as the change over the same month a year earlier.
terms.formula: Inflation % = (Index this month ÷ Index a year earlier − 1) × 100

terms.meaning: An agency's grade of a borrower's ability to repay, from AAA (highest) down to D (default). Indian agencies include CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings.
Indian units for large numbers: 1 lakh is 1,00,000 (one hundred thousand) and 1 crore is 1,00,00,000 (ten million). 100 lakh make a crore, and 1 lakh crore is ₹1 trillion.
terms.formula: 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10 million

terms.meaning: Current assets divided by current liabilities: can the company pay bills due within a year from assets it will turn into cash within a year?
terms.formula: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

terms.meaning: The final issue price fixed after bidding. Retail, employee and shareholder applicants may tick 'cut-off' to accept whatever price is set.
The checks FinLit runs before publishing a report: statements reconcile, ratios are recalculated at today's price, dates line up and bad price points are removed.

A mutual fund that invests in bonds, government securities and money-market instruments. SEBI's debt categories are set by duration (overnight, liquid, short, medium and long duration), by credit quality (corporate bond, credit risk, banking and PSU) or by issuer (gilt), plus floater and dynamic bond funds.

terms.term: Debt to assets and liabilities to assets
terms.meaning: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
Total debt divided by yearly free cash flow: how many years of spare cash it would take to repay all debt.
How many days, on average, customers take to pay.
terms.formula: Debtor days = Receivables ÷ Revenue × 365

terms.meaning: Total borrowings divided by shareholders' equity: how much the company has borrowed for every rupee owners have put in. Some sources use total liabilities instead of borrowings.
terms.formula: D/E = Total debt ÷ Shareholders' equity

terms.meaning: Defensive sectors sell things people buy in good times and bad, such as food, medicines and power. Cyclical sectors, such as autos, metals, property and capital goods, rise and fall with the economy.
An electronic account that holds your shares and other securities, like a bank account holds money. It is opened through a broker or bank with a depository (NSDL or CDSL).
When a company separates one of its businesses into a new listed company, and shareholders receive shares of the new company in a set ratio.
aliases: Demerged: you now hold all its parts

terms.meaning: Spreading the cost of a physical asset, such as a machine, over the years it is used, as a yearly expense.
terms.formula: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life

terms.meaning: Contracts whose value comes from another asset, such as a share or index. Futures and options are the most common.
Earnings per share after counting shares that could be created from options, warrants and convertible bonds, which spreads the profit over more shares.
terms.formula: Diluted EPS = Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ Diluted weighted average shares

terms.meaning: The fall in existing owners' percentage stake when a company issues new shares.
The version of a mutual fund you buy straight from the fund house, with no distributor in between, so no distribution commission is paid out of the fund.
A business the company has sold, closed or decided to sell. Its profit or loss is shown on a separate line, apart from the continuing operations.

The discount rate is the yearly return an investor requires, used to turn future cash into today's money. Present value is what a future amount is worth today, and the discount factor is the multiplier that gets there.
terms.formula: Present value = Future cash ÷ (1 + r)^n; Discount factor = 1 ÷ (1 + r)^n

terms.meaning: A valuation method that estimates a company's future free cash flows and converts them to today's value using a discount rate.
Spreading money across different companies, sectors and asset types so one bad outcome does not sink the whole portfolio.
A share of company profit paid to shareholders, usually in cash. Indian companies declare interim dividends during the year and a final dividend after the annual results.
terms.formula: Dividend yield = Yearly dividend per share ÷ Share price

terms.meaning: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
terms.formula: Payout ratio % = Dividend per share ÷ EPS × 100

terms.meaning: The total dividend paid in a year divided by the number of shares.
Yearly dividend per share as a percentage of the current share price.
terms.formula: Dividend yield % = Dividend per share ÷ Share price × 100

terms.meaning: Indian mutual funds, insurance companies, banks and pension funds that invest in shares.
How much of a yardstick's falls a fund went through, in percent, measured over the periods when the yardstick fell. 80% means the fund fell 8% when the yardstick fell 10%.
terms.formula: Downside capture = Fund return in down periods ÷ Yardstick return in down periods × 100
aliases: How it behaved when similar funds fell

terms.meaning: A measure like volatility that counts only the falls: days with gains count as zero.
terms.formula: Downside deviation = √(Average of min(Daily return, 0)²) × √252

terms.meaning: The fall from a previous peak to a later low, in percent. FinLit's 'distance from the running high' chart shows it over time.
The first detailed offer document a company files with SEBI before an IPO, describing its business, finances, risks and the proposed issue.

A way of splitting return on equity into three parts: net margin (profit per ₹100 of sales), asset turnover (sales per ₹1 of assets) and the equity multiplier (assets per ₹1 of equity). The five-step version also splits out the tax burden and the interest burden.
terms.formula: ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier; five-step: (PAT ÷ PBT) × (PBT ÷ EBIT) × EBIT margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier

terms.meaning: For a bond or debt fund, roughly how much its price changes when interest rates move: with a modified duration of 4 years, a 1-point rise in rates cuts the price by about 4%. It also reflects the average time until its cash flows are received.
terms.formula: Price change % ≈ −Modified duration × Change in yield (percentage points)

terms.meaning: A call where management presents results and answers questions from analysts and investors. The transcript is the written record, filed with the exchanges.
The company's net profit divided by the number of shares: how much profit each share 'earns'.
terms.formula: EPS = (Net profit − Preference dividends) ÷ Weighted average shares

terms.meaning: How far reported profit reflects the steady, cash-backed earning power of the business, rather than one-offs, accounting choices or borrowing.
The inverse of P/E: yearly profit per share as a percentage of the share price.
terms.formula: Earnings yield % = EPS ÷ Share price × 100

terms.meaning: EBIT is Earnings Before Interest and Tax: profit after depreciation but before interest and tax. EBIT margin is EBIT as a share of revenue.
terms.formula: EBIT margin % = EBIT ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization: operating profit before the cost of borrowing and wear on assets.
terms.formula: EBITDA = Net income + Interest + Taxes + Depreciation + Amortization

terms.meaning: EBITDA as a share of revenue.
terms.formula: EBITDA margin % = EBITDA ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: The tax a company actually paid as a share of its profit before tax.
terms.formula: Effective tax rate % = Tax expense ÷ Profit before tax × 100

terms.meaning: A monthly index of output in eight basic industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity.
An equity mutual fund with a three-year lock-in that qualifies for a tax deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh a year under Section 80C in the old income tax regime.
A fixed monthly payment that repays a loan's interest and principal over its term.
A portion set aside for the company's employees, often at a discount, with a bid limit of ₹5 lakh (₹2 lakh initially, more only if the portion is undersubscribed).
The value of the whole business to everyone with a claim on it: market cap plus debt, minus cash.
terms.formula: EV = Market cap + Total debt − Cash and equivalents

terms.meaning: An index in which every share counts the same, whatever its size, instead of in proportion to its market value.
terms.formula: Equal-weighted return = Average of each share's return

terms.meaning: What would be left for shareholders if the company sold all its assets and paid all its liabilities: the owners' stake. The word also means shares in general.
terms.formula: Equity = Assets − Liabilities

terms.meaning: A fund, often tracking an index, that trades on the stock exchange like a share.
Enterprise value divided by EBITDA.
terms.formula: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA

terms.meaning: Enterprise value divided by revenue (EV/Sales) or by operating cash flow (EV/CFO).
Unusual, one-time gains or losses, such as selling a factory or paying a large fine.
A disclosure a listed company must send to the stock exchanges, such as results, board decisions, orders won, ratings or legal matters.
The price of one currency in another; for India usually the number of rupees needed to buy one US dollar.
The cut-off: if you buy on or after this date you do not get the upcoming dividend. The share price usually drops by roughly the dividend amount that morning.
A fee a fund charges, as a percentage of the amount, if you sell units within a stated period after buying them.
terms.formula: Amount received = Units × NAV × (1 − Exit load %)

terms.meaning: A way to set a DCF's terminal value by multiplying the last forecast year's cash flow, or profit, by a chosen multiple, instead of assuming growth for ever.
terms.formula: Terminal value = Final-year FCF × Exit multiple

terms.meaning: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of your investment.
terms.formula: Expense ratio = Fund operating costs ÷ Average net assets

terms.meaning: All the costs of running the business: raw materials, staff, rent, power, marketing and so on.

The last day a futures or options contract trades, after which it is settled. Index options in India have weekly and monthly expiries and stock contracts monthly ones, on days set by the exchanges within SEBI's rules.
A moving average that gives more weight to recent prices, so it turns sooner than a simple average of the same length. EMA 20 is the 20-day exponential average.
terms.formula: EMA today = Price × k + EMA yesterday × (1 − k), where k = 2 ÷ (n + 1)

terms.meaning: The nominal value of a share printed in the company's records, such as ₹1, ₹2 or ₹10. It has nothing to do with the market price.
An ETF that follows an index built by a rule instead of by company size, such as momentum, quality, value, low volatility or equal weight.
Free cash flow as a percentage of market cap: the spare cash the business generates for each ₹100 of its market value.
terms.formula: FCF yield % = Free cash flow ÷ Market cap × 100

terms.meaning: Horizontal levels drawn at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of a price move, which some chart readers use to mark where a pullback might pause.
terms.formula: Level = High − (High − Low) × Ratio

terms.meaning: The value of shares foreign institutions (FIIs or FPIs) and domestic institutions (DIIs, such as mutual funds and insurers) bought, minus what they sold, in the cash market each day, in ₹ crore.
terms.formula: Net flow = Buy value − Sell value

terms.meaning: Total assets divided by shareholders' equity.
terms.formula: Financial leverage = Total assets ÷ Shareholders' equity

terms.meaning: FinLit's 0–100 summary of a company's health: the average of five pillar scores, each built from ratios scored against fixed thresholds.
FinLit's estimates of a company's revenue and net profit for the next 1, 3 or 5 years, worked out from its own reported growth and its sector's.
terms.formula: Next year = This year × (1 + Weighted growth rate)

terms.meaning: FinLit's advanced financial-health rating of a listed company, part of the Gold plan. It scores four parts from the company's filings and prices (Growth & Profitability, Valuation, Quality and Risk) and combines them into a score out of 100 with a label: Strong (80 and above), Healthy (65 to 79), Average (50 to 64), Weak (35 to 49) or Poor (below 35).
terms.formula: Prism score = 0.40 × Growth & Profitability + 0.30 × Valuation + 0.20 × Quality + 0.10 × Risk

terms.meaning: The 12-month period used for accounts and tax. In India it runs from 1 April to 31 March, so FY26 means April 2025 to March 2026.
A long-term physical asset used to run the business, such as land, buildings or machinery, not meant to be sold.
Revenue divided by fixed assets such as plant and machinery.
An account number a fund house gives an investor; one person can have several folios. A fund's or category's folio count is the number of such accounts.
The foreign currency assets, gold, special drawing rights (SDRs) and IMF reserve position held by the RBI.
Overseas funds, banks and investors buying Indian shares, now officially called foreign portfolio investors (FPIs).
A public offer of shares by a company that is already listed.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: the spare cash left after keeping and growing the business.
terms.formula: FCF = Operating cash flow − Capital expenditure

terms.meaning: Shares available for trading by the public, excluding promoter and other locked-in holdings.
New shares created and sold in an IPO. The money raised goes to the company.
The group SEBI places a mutual fund scheme in according to what it invests in, such as Large Cap, Mid Cap, Liquid or Gilt. AMFI lists every scheme under its category.
Money coming into a fund or category from new investments, minus money going out through redemptions, over a period.
terms.formula: Net flow = Money invested − Money redeemed

terms.meaning: The company that sets up and manages mutual fund schemes, called an asset management company (AMC), for example Axis Mutual Fund or HDFC Mutual Fund.
The person or team at a fund house who decides what an actively managed fund holds, within its stated rules.
A mutual fund that invests in other mutual funds or ETFs instead of buying shares or bonds directly, for example to hold overseas funds or a ready mix of funds.
aliases: Others: Fund of funds and the rest

terms.meaning: The fundamental score uses only the business's statements; the technical score uses only the price chart. FinLit never blends the two without showing both.
An agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date, traded on an exchange.

terms.term: Gold and silver units (tola, sovereign, troy ounce)
terms.meaning: Units used to price precious metals. A tola is about 11.66 grams, a sovereign (pavan) is 8 grams, and a troy ounce, the international unit, is about 31.10 grams.
terms.formula: 1 troy ounce = 31.1034768 g; 1 tola = 11.6638038 g; 1 sovereign = 8 g

terms.meaning: An ETF whose price follows the domestic price of gold or silver, and which holds the metal for its investors.
An intangible asset created when one company buys another for more than the fair value of its assets minus liabilities. The extra amount is goodwill.
terms.formula: Goodwill = Purchase price − Fair value of net assets

terms.meaning: A rough fair value per share from the investor Benjamin Graham's formula, using EPS and book value per share.
terms.formula: Graham number = √(22.5 × EPS × Book value per share)

terms.meaning: An option allowing the issue to be increased by up to 15% to stabilise the price after listing.
The unofficial premium at which IPO shares are said to trade informally before listing.
A non-performing asset (NPA) is a loan unpaid for 90 days or more. Gross NPA is the total; net NPA is after setting aside provisions.
The total value of goods and services produced in a country in a period.
terms.formula: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government spending + (Exports − Imports)

terms.meaning: The share of revenue left after the direct cost of making the product or delivering the service.
terms.formula: Gross margin % = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: The choice under which a fund keeps all its earnings invested, so no money is paid out and the NAV rises as the investments grow.
Shares of a company expected to grow sales and profit faster than the market, often paying small or no dividends.
An ETF that holds government bonds, for example 5-year or 10-year benchmark G-Secs, and follows a government bond index.
A grid in which colour shows the size of each value, such as one square per trading day or one cell per month and year.
An investment made to reduce the risk of loss in another, for example buying a put option on shares you own.
A measure of concentration: the sum of the squared weights of every holding or sector, from close to 0 (spread over many) to 1 (everything in one).
terms.formula: HHI = Sum of (Weight)², with weights as fractions of 1

terms.meaning: The total return over the time you held an investment, including income.
terms.formula: HPR = (Income + End value − Start value) ÷ Start value

terms.meaning: The minimum return an investment or project must earn to be worth doing.

A mutual fund that holds both shares and debt, and sometimes gold or other assets. SEBI's hybrid categories include conservative, balanced and aggressive hybrid, dynamic asset allocation (balanced advantage), multi-asset allocation, arbitrage and equity savings funds.

The choice under which a fund pays out part of its value to you from time to time. It replaced the older name 'dividend option'. 'Payout' sends the money to you; 'reinvestment' buys more units with it.
A monthly index of output from mining, manufacturing and electricity, published by MoSPI.
The share price a scenario arrives at: projected EPS multiplied by the assumed target P/E.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Current EPS × (1 + g)^n × Target P/E

terms.meaning: The volatility that, put into an option pricing model, gives the option's current market price. It is the market's price for the swings it expects, stated per year.
An estimate of what an imported commodity should cost in India: the international price converted at the exchange rate, plus customs duty.
terms.formula: Import parity ≈ International price × Exchange rate × (1 + Customs duty)

terms.term: In the money, at the money and out of the money
terms.meaning: A call is in the money when its strike is below the current price, and a put when its strike is above it. At the money means the strike is at or next to the current price; out of the money is the opposite of in the money.
terms.formula: Call intrinsic value = max(Price − Strike, 0); Put intrinsic value = max(Strike − Price, 0)

terms.meaning: A number that tracks the combined price of a chosen basket of stocks, such as the 50 largest companies on the NSE.
A mutual fund or ETF that simply copies an index such as the Nifty 50, at low cost.
The price-to-earnings ratio of a whole index, such as the Nifty 50, from the combined market value and earnings of its companies. An index's P/B and dividend yield work the same way.
terms.formula: Index P/E = Combined market value of members ÷ Combined earnings of members

terms.meaning: The NSE's 'fear gauge': the volatility the options market expects in the Nifty over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.
The rate at which prices in general rise, reducing what money can buy. In India it is usually tracked by the consumer price index (CPI).
terms.formula: Inflation % = (CPI now − CPI a year ago) ÷ CPI a year ago × 100

terms.meaning: Insolvency is when a company cannot pay its debts. India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) sets a process to revive or sell such companies.
A bank's interest expense as a share of its total income; a FinLit screener filter for lenders.
Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times over the company can pay its interest.
terms.formula: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest expense

terms.meaning: An interim dividend is declared during the financial year; a final dividend is proposed after the year ends and approved at the annual general meeting.
The yearly return at which the present value of an investment's cash flows equals zero.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_t ÷ (1 + IRR)^t

terms.meaning: An intraday trade is bought and sold on the same day; a delivery trade means the shares move into your demat account and you hold them.

terms.term: Intrinsic value and margin of safety
terms.meaning: Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a business is really worth based on its future cash flows. Margin of safety is the gap when the price is well below that estimate.
How many days, on average, goods sit in stock before being sold.
terms.formula: Inventory days = Inventory ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods the company holds but has not yet sold.

IPO shares are split into reserved portions for different types of investor: qualified institutional buyers (QIB), non-institutional investors (NII) and retail individual investors (RII), plus optional employee and shareholder quotas.
Slides a company publishes with its results or at events, summarising performance, strategy and outlook.
The first time a company sells its shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.
International Securities Identification Number: a 12-character code that identifies one security, or one plan and option of a mutual fund, worldwide.
The final price per share at which the IPO shares are allotted.
The total value of shares offered in the IPO, fresh issue and offer for sale together, such as ₹837 crore.
A business set up by two or more partners who share control, costs and profits while staying separate companies.
The first record of a transaction in a company's books, showing the same amount as a debit in one account and a credit in another.
terms.formula: Total debits = Total credits

terms.meaning: A bond with a low credit rating, paying higher interest because the risk of default is higher.
An illegal practice of moving money between accounts to exploit clearing delays and create fake balances.
A number that tracks how well a business is doing on what matters most, such as same-store sales for a retailer or users for a telecom firm.
Mandatory identity and address checks before opening a bank, demat, broker or mutual fund account.

terms.term: Large cap, mid cap and small cap
terms.meaning: Size groups based on market value. In India, the 100 largest listed companies are large caps, the next 150 mid caps, and the rest small caps; the smallest are often called micro caps.

terms.term: Last traded price (LTP) and closing price
terms.meaning: The LTP is the price of the most recent trade. The closing price is the official price at the end of the trading day, calculated by the exchange from the last half hour of trades.
aliases: Last traded price and closing price

terms.meaning: The investment bank that manages the IPO: due diligence, pricing, marketing and paperwork.
A FinLit flag for a stock that closes at a 52-week high while its industry is still well below its own high. A full flag means the industry is further down; an early flag, less far.
FinLit's plain description of how a share's last 12 months compare with its closest peers, measured against the peer group's sector index: Leader, In line or Laggard.
Using borrowed money to increase the size of a business or an investment. It magnifies both gains and losses.
terms.formula: Leverage ratio = Total debt ÷ Total equity

terms.meaning: Money or obligations a company owes to others: loans, unpaid bills, taxes due, customer advances.
terms.formula: Liabilities = Assets − Equity

terms.term: Liquid ETF (1-day rate or overnight ETF)
terms.meaning: An ETF that lends money for one day at a time, for example to banks through overnight lending, and so holds very short-term debt.

terms.term: Liquid fund and money market fund
terms.meaning: Debt funds that hold very short-term instruments: liquid funds hold securities maturing in up to 91 days, and money market funds hold money-market instruments maturing in up to a year.
How quickly something can be turned into cash without losing value. For a company, its ability to meet short-term bills; for a stock, how easily it can be bought or sold.
The listing date is when IPO shares start trading. Listing gain or loss is the difference between the first trading price and the issue price.
The loan amount as a percentage of the value of the asset securing it, such as a house or gold.
terms.formula: LTV % = Loan amount ÷ Asset value × 100

terms.meaning: A period during which certain shareholders cannot sell. Promoters' minimum stake of 20% is generally locked for 18 months, the rest for 6 months, along with most pre-IPO investors.
Only borrowings due after more than a year, divided by equity.
The minimum number of shares you can bid for, and the steps your bid must come in. SEBI sets it so one lot costs roughly ₹10,000 to ₹15,000 on the mainboard.
Investing an amount all at once, instead of in instalments.
terms.formula: Future value = Amount × (1 + r)^n

terms.meaning: The gap between the 12-day and the 26-day EMA of the price. Its own 9-day EMA is the signal line, and the histogram is MACD minus the signal line.
terms.formula: MACD = EMA 12 − EMA 26; Signal line = EMA 9 of MACD; Histogram = MACD − Signal line

terms.meaning: An IPO by a larger company that lists on the main NSE and BSE platforms.
A share of revenue kept as profit at some level, such as gross, operating or net margin. In trading, 'margin' can also mean money borrowed from a broker to buy shares.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net income ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: How many stocks rose versus fell on a day, for example '91 rose, 424 fell'.
The total market value of a company: share price multiplied by the number of shares.
terms.formula: Market cap = Share price × Shares outstanding

terms.meaning: A broker required to quote buy and sell prices in an SME stock for at least three years after listing.
A market order buys or sells straight away at the best price available. A limit order sets the worst price you will accept and waits until it can be filled at that price or better.
The date when a bond, deposit or loan's principal is repaid.
The strike price at which option buyers, taken together, would receive the smallest total payout if the underlying expired there.
An open standard that lets AI assistants, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, call outside data sources. FinLit offers a free, read-only MCP connection to its Indian stock, fund and market data.
India's main commodity derivatives exchange, where futures on gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas and base metals trade.
The middle value when numbers are lined up in order; half are above it and half below.
A robust measure of spread: the median of how far each value is from the median. Unlike the standard deviation, one extreme value hardly changes it.
terms.formula: MAD = Median of |Value − Median|
aliases: Unusual year: far from this row's other years

terms.meaning: The smallest amount needed to apply: one lot at the upper end of the price band.
The speed and strength of recent price moves.
The six-member committee that sets the RBI's repo rate. It meets at least four times a year, in practice about every two months.
The share of months in a period, such as the last 36, in which a fund's return beat the median of its category.
terms.formula: Months ahead % = Months above the category median ÷ Months counted × 100

terms.meaning: The average closing price over the last 50 or 200 trading days, redrawn each day. An EMA (exponential moving average) gives recent days more weight.
terms.formula: Simple moving average = Sum of last n closes ÷ n

terms.meaning: A fund that pools money from many investors and is managed by a professional fund manager, investing in shares, bonds or both.

FinLit's 0 to 100 score of a mutual fund against funds of the same kind, built from four parts: Performance, Risk, Cost and Quality (age, size and how the portfolio is built). How much each part counts depends on the fund group and stays with the model.
terms.formula: Score combines Performance, Risk, Cost and Quality

terms.meaning: A company that lends money or provides financial services but does not hold a full banking licence, such as Bajaj Finance.
The value of one unit of a mutual fund, calculated at the end of each business day.
terms.formula: NAV = (Assets − Liabilities) ÷ Units outstanding

terms.meaning: Total debt minus cash and equivalents. A negative figure means net cash.
terms.formula: Net debt = Total debt − Cash and equivalents

terms.meaning: Net debt divided by yearly EBITDA: roughly how many years of operating profit it would take to repay the debt.
terms.formula: Net debt to EBITDA = Net debt ÷ EBITDA

terms.meaning: Profit left after every expense, interest and tax: the 'bottom line'. Often called PAT, profit after tax.
terms.formula: Net income = Revenue − All expenses (including interest, depreciation and tax)

terms.meaning: Net interest income is interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings. Net interest margin (NIM) is that figure as a share of interest-earning assets.
terms.formula: NIM % = Net interest income ÷ Average interest-earning assets × 100

terms.meaning: The share of revenue that ends up as net profit after every cost and tax.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100
aliases: Net margin change, year on year

terms.meaning: Future cash flows converted into today's money, minus the upfront cost.
terms.formula: NPV = Sum of CF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t − Initial investment

terms.meaning: What a person or company owns minus what it owes. For a company it is the same as shareholders' equity.
terms.formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total liabilities

terms.meaning: India's two headline indices. The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the NSE; the Sensex tracks 30 large companies on BSE.
Individuals, companies and trusts applying for more than ₹2 lakh. Split into small NII (₹2 lakh to ₹10 lakh, one third of the portion) and big NII (above ₹10 lakh, two thirds).
A bond issued by an Indian company that cannot be converted into shares. Reliance, for example, allotted NCDs of ₹1 lakh face value each in October 2026.
Profit with one-off items taken out, and the return on equity worked out from that profit, to show what the business earns in a usual year.
terms.formula: Normalized profit = Reported net profit − One-off items × (1 − Tax rate on one-offs)

terms.meaning: Operating cash flow as a percentage of revenue: how many rupees of cash the business brings in from each ₹100 of sales.
terms.formula: OCF margin % = Operating cash flow ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: Existing shareholders, such as promoters or private-equity funds, selling their shares in an IPO. The money goes to them, not the company. Listed companies' promoters can also sell through a special 'OFS window' on the exchanges.
A running total that adds the day's volume when the price closes up and subtracts it when the price closes down.
terms.formula: OBV today = OBV yesterday + Volume (on an up close) or − Volume (on a down close)

terms.meaning: The number of futures or option contracts that are still open, not yet closed or settled, at the end of a day.
terms.formula: OI change = Open interest today − Open interest the day before

terms.meaning: An open-ended fund takes in and pays out money every business day at the NAV. A closed-ended fund raises money once, runs for a fixed term and can be sold only on the stock exchange or when it matures. An interval fund opens only at set times.
Cash generated by the main business in a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes.
The share of revenue left after operating costs, before interest and tax.
terms.formula: Operating margin % = Operating profit ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: Profit from the core business: revenue minus operating costs, before interest, depreciation, tax and other income. FinLit's P&L shows it this way, which is close to EBITDA.
The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose something.
terms.formula: Opportunity cost = Return on best option given up − Return on chosen option

terms.meaning: A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a fixed price before expiry.
A table of all the call and put options on one underlying for an expiry date, strike by strike, with each option's price, open interest, volume and implied volatility.
Income that does not come from the main business, such as interest on cash, dividends from investments or gains from selling assets.
Overbought means the price has risen fast and may pause or pull back; oversold means it has fallen fast and may bounce.
A facility that lets you withdraw more than your account balance, up to a limit, paying interest on what you use.
An ETF listed in India that holds shares listed abroad, such as the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 or Hang Seng companies.
Oversubscription means bids exceed the shares offered; undersubscription means they fall short.
How many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers.
terms.formula: Payable days = Payables ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Companies in the same industry used for comparison.
The P/E ratio divided by the expected or recent EPS growth rate.
terms.formula: PEG = P/E ÷ EPS growth rate (%)

terms.meaning: A percentage point is the plain difference between two percentages: a rise from 10% to 12% is 2 percentage points, but a 20% increase. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point.
terms.formula: 1 percentage point = 100 basis points

terms.meaning: A percentile says what share of a group sits below a value: the 90th percentile is higher than 90% of the group. A rank orders the group from first to last.
terms.formula: Percentile = Number of values below ÷ Number of values × 100

terms.meaning: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.

terms.term: Pillars (Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical)
terms.meaning: The five areas FinLit IQs. Quality covers returns on capital and how well profit turns into cash; Growth covers sales and profit growth; Profitability covers margins and how hard assets work; Balance sheet covers how much of the assets are funded by liabilities and whether profit is backed by cash; Technical covers the price trend.
aliases: Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical

terms.meaning: All the investments a person or institution holds.
Preference shares pay a fixed dividend that must be paid before ordinary shareholders get anything, and rank ahead of them if the company is wound up. That fixed payout is the preference dividend.
terms.formula: Profit for ordinary shareholders = Net profit − Preference dividends

terms.meaning: Shares sold privately to selected investors shortly before the IPO, at a negotiated price.
How far an ETF's exchange price is above (premium) or below (discount) the net asset value of its underlying holdings on the same day.
terms.formula: Premium / discount = (Exchange close ÷ NAV − 1) × 100

terms.meaning: Profit before tax as a share of revenue.
terms.formula: Pre-tax margin % = Profit before tax ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.term: Price band (floor price and cap price)
terms.meaning: The range within which investors may bid in a book-built IPO, such as ₹1,065 to ₹1,119. The lower end is the floor, the upper end the cap.

A jump in price between two sessions that leaves an empty space on the chart, because the day opened above the previous high or below the previous low. A breakaway gap starts a new move; an exhaustion gap comes late in a long one.
The change in a price between two dates, as a percentage, without adding dividends or other payouts received in between.
terms.formula: Price return = (Latest price ÷ Earlier price − 1) × 100

terms.term: Price to cash flow and price to free cash flow
terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly operating cash flow (P/CFO) or by free cash flow (P/FCF).
terms.formula: P/FCF = Market cap ÷ Free cash flow

terms.meaning: The share price divided by book value per share: what you pay for each rupee of net assets.
terms.formula: P/B = Share price ÷ Book value per share

terms.meaning: The share price divided by EPS: how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.
terms.formula: P/E = Share price ÷ EPS

terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly revenue.
terms.formula: P/S = Market cap ÷ Revenue

terms.meaning: The primary market is where new shares are first sold, as in an IPO. The secondary market is the stock exchange, where investors trade existing shares with each other.
The original amount borrowed or invested, not counting interest or returns.
terms.formula: Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: The report of a company's income and costs over a period, ending in its profit. Also called the income statement.
Profit after all expenses, interest and depreciation, but before income tax.
A section of FinLit's company report that tests how far profit and ROE reflect the business: one-off items, normalized profit and ROE, the DuPont breakdown and whether profit is backed by cash.
The founders, family or parent company that control a listed company.
Promoter holding is the share of the company the promoter group owns. A pledge is when promoters use their shares as security for a loan.
The final offer document, filed after the price is fixed, with the issue price and final size.
The share of bad loans a bank has already set money aside for.

A FinLit Prism rating given on less evidence than a full one: coverage is between 50% and 80%, or there are fewer than six comparable quarters to judge the sales and profit record. A provisional rating is never higher than Healthy.
A short fall within a larger uptrend, or a short rise within a downtrend, before the main trend carries on.
Total open interest in put options divided by total open interest in call options, across every strike of an expiry. PCR by volume uses the day's traded volume instead.
terms.formula: PCR = Total put open interest ÷ Total call open interest

terms.meaning: The chance of seeing a link at least as strong as the one measured if there were in fact no link at all. A small p-value means the pattern is unlikely to be pure chance.
Large professional investors such as mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, pension funds and registered foreign portfolio investors.
A quick way for a listed company to raise money by selling new shares only to qualified institutional buyers.
A central bank buying large amounts of government bonds or other securities to push money into the economy and lower long-term interest rates.
Where a stock's 6-month return ranks among the counted stocks of its industry: top quarter, 2nd, 3rd or bottom quarter.
Financial results listed companies publish every three months, within 45 days of the quarter's end (60 days for the full year).
The change in a figure compared with the immediately preceding quarter.
aliases: Operating profit growth, quarter on quarter

terms.meaning: A FinLit tool where you type a screening rule, such as Market cap > 500 AND P/E < 15, and get every listed Indian company that matches.
Like the current ratio but leaving out inventory, which may be slow to sell.
terms.formula: Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities

terms.meaning: An interest rate minus inflation.
terms.formula: Real rate ≈ Nominal rate − Inflation

terms.meaning: The profit or loss on investments you have actually sold, from the buying and selling prices. Gross P&L is before charges and taxes; net P&L is after them.
terms.formula: Realised P&L = (Sell price − Buy price) × Quantity − Charges

terms.meaning: Bringing a portfolio back to its target mix by trimming what has grown and adding to what has shrunk.
A way to chart several series from the same starting point: each is divided by its own first value and multiplied by 100. A reading of 130 means a 30% rise since the start.
terms.formula: Rebased value = Value ÷ First value × 100

terms.meaning: The date on which you must be on the company's list of shareholders to receive a dividend, bonus or split.

FinLit screener filters for warning signs: loss-making, negative operating cash flow, profit not backed by cash, high debt, weak interest cover, profit falling sharply, promoters selling and a price far below its long-term trend.
Release of blocked money for shares not allotted.
The firm that processes IPO applications, decides allotment under SEBI rules and handles refunds.
The straight line that best fits a scatter of points. The slope is how much Y changes for each 1-unit rise in X; the intercept is the value of Y where the line crosses X = 0.
terms.formula: Y = Intercept + Slope × X

terms.meaning: The version of a mutual fund bought through a distributor or advisor. A commission for them is paid out of the fund, so its yearly cost is higher than the Direct plan's.
A disclosure made under Regulation 30 of SEBI's listing rules (LODR), which requires companies to report material events promptly.
A share's return minus the return of an index over the same period, in percentage points. Positive means the share did better than the index. It is different from RSI.
terms.formula: Relative return = Share's return − Index return

terms.meaning: Comparing a company's valuation ratio with its own past (for example its 5-year median P/E) or with the median of its sector.
The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term money to banks. It is the RBI's main policy rate.

The results season is the few weeks after each quarter ends, when most listed companies report. The results calendar lists the board-meeting dates companies have announced for approving their results.
Individuals and other non-institutional holders, grouped as 'public' in the shareholding pattern.
Profit a company has kept over the years instead of paying it out as dividends.
terms.formula: Retained earnings = Opening balance + Net income − Dividends

terms.meaning: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
terms.formula: Retention ratio % = 100 − Payout ratio %

terms.meaning: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
terms.formula: ROA % = Net profit ÷ Total assets × 100

terms.meaning: Operating profit (EBIT) earned for every ₹100 of total capital used in the business, from both shareholders and lenders.
terms.formula: ROCE % = EBIT ÷ (Shareholders' equity + Debt) × 100

terms.meaning: How much profit a company makes for every ₹100 its shareholders have put in and left in the business.
terms.formula: ROE % = Net profit ÷ Average shareholders' equity × 100

terms.meaning: The gain or loss on an investment as a share of what it cost.
terms.formula: ROI % = Net gain ÷ Cost of investment × 100

terms.meaning: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
terms.formula: Return on tangible assets % = Net profit ÷ (Total assets − Intangible assets) × 100

terms.meaning: The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before any costs are taken out. Also called sales, turnover or the 'top line'.
A DCF run backwards: it starts from today's share price and works out the growth that price implies.
The updated offer document filed before the IPO opens, with almost everything except the final price and number of shares.
An offer to existing shareholders to buy new shares, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they already hold.
An individual applying for up to ₹2 lakh in an IPO.
How much risk you can and are willing to take, based on your age, income, goals, time horizon and temperament.
The return on an investment considered to carry almost no risk, usually the yield on Indian government Treasury bills or bonds.
SEBI's six-level label of a mutual fund's risk, from Low to Very High, which every fund must show and review each month, next to the risk-o-meter of its benchmark.
A way of fitting a line that takes the median of the slopes between every pair of points instead of using least squares. A few extreme points barely move it.
terms.formula: Theil-Sen slope = Median of (Yj − Yi) ÷ (Xj − Xi) over all pairs of points

terms.meaning: Returns measured over every window of a fixed length, for example every one-year period ending on each day, instead of over a single start and end date.

terms.term: Rotation corners (Ahead and gaining, Ahead but slowing, Behind and slipping, Behind but gaining)
terms.meaning: Where an industry sits on two numbers measured against the average industry: its 6-month return (ahead or behind) and its last month's return (gaining or slowing).
A weekly ranking of NSE industry groups by how far they have run ahead of the average industry, over several periods, with breadth added.
A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a stock has risen versus fallen over the last 14 days.
The share of the ups and downs in one measure that a straight line through another measure accounts for, from 0% to 100%. For a simple line it equals the correlation squared.
terms.formula: R² = 1 − (Sum of squared residuals ÷ Total sum of squares)

terms.meaning: Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
How fast revenue and net profit have grown, usually shown for the last year and as 3-year and 5-year CAGRs.
aliases: Gap between sales and profit growth

terms.term: Scenario analysis (bear, base and bull cases)
terms.meaning: Working out a value or result under several sets of assumptions, such as a bear, a base and a bull case, sometimes with a probability for each to give a weighted figure.
terms.formula: Weighted value = Sum of (Case value × Probability)

terms.meaning: FinLit's labels for score ranges: Strong 78 and above, Healthy 62 to 77, Mixed 45 to 61, Watch below 45.
A tool that lists every company matching rules you set, such as 'P/E below 20 and ROE above 15%'.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India: the government body that regulates stock markets, brokers, mutual funds, research analysts and investment advisers.
A sector is a broad part of the economy, such as Financial Services or Energy. An industry is a narrower group inside it, such as Private Sector Bank or Refineries & Marketing.
An ETF that follows an index of one sector, such as banks or IT, or one theme, such as defence or manufacturing.
Industries taking turns to lead the market. FinLit measures it against the average industry: every NSE industry or sector group with a reading, weighted equally.

terms.term: Sector signal states (Washout, Thrust, Confirmed, Fading)
terms.meaning: FinLit's labels for where an NSE industry stands in its breadth cycle: Washout (broad selling), Thrust (a broad rebound), Confirmed (most stocks trending up together) and Fading (breadth breaking down).
Equity funds that invest at least 80% in one sector, such as banking or pharma, or one theme, such as defence, technology or consumption.

terms.term: Sectoral index (Nifty Bank, Nifty IT and others)
terms.meaning: An index that tracks the shares of one sector or theme, such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma or Nifty Auto.
The umbrella word for financial instruments that can be bought and sold: shares, bonds, mutual fund units and derivatives.
The breakdown of revenue and profit by business line or region, such as Oil-to-Chemicals, Retail and Digital for Reliance.
A table that shows how a result changes as one or two inputs change, such as the value per share for each pair of discount rate and growth rate.
The process of handing over shares and money after a trade. In India most trades settle one working day after the trade date (T+1).
A portion reserved for shareholders of a listed parent or group company, usually up to 10% of the issue. Insurers sometimes reserve a policyholder portion in the same way.
The quarterly breakdown of who owns a company's shares: promoters, foreign institutions, domestic institutions, government and the public.
Return earned above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility.
terms.formula: Sharpe = (Return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation
aliases: Return for each unit of price swing

terms.meaning: Interest calculated only on the original principal.
terms.formula: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, in a mutual fund.
An IPO by a small or medium company that lists on a separate platform, NSE Emerge or BSE SME.
A SEBI category of funds built around a goal, retirement funds and children's funds, with a lock-in of at least five years or until retirement age or the child comes of age, whichever is earlier.
A company's ability to meet all its long-term obligations and keep operating.
A price-discovery session on listing day, when orders are collected and a fair opening price is set before normal trading usually begins at 10 am.
A chart with one spoke per measure, each running from weaker at the centre to stronger at the edge, joined into a shape. Several companies can be drawn on top of each other.

A way of describing where a share is in its price cycle using a long moving average: Stage 1 basing (the average flat), Stage 2 advancing (price above a rising average), Stage 3 topping (flat again after a rise) and Stage 4 declining (price below a falling average).
A measure of how spread out values are around their average. In a roughly bell-shaped spread, about two-thirds of values lie within one standard deviation of the average.
terms.formula: Standard deviation = √(Average of (Value − Mean)²)

terms.meaning: A SIP whose instalment rises each year, by a fixed amount or a percentage, for example in line with pay rises.
terms.formula: Instalment in year n = First instalment × (1 + Step-up %)^(n − 1)

terms.meaning: A regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade securities. India's two main exchanges are the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange).
A small piece of ownership in a company. Owning one share of a company with 100 crore shares means you own one part in 100 crore of it.
Dividing each share into smaller units, for example one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares. The price per share falls in proportion.
An order that sells automatically if the price falls to a level you choose.
Plain-language findings FinLit draws from a company's numbers, such as 'profit backed by cash' or 'price below its long-term trend'.
The price at which an option lets its buyer buy the underlying (a call) or sell it (a put).
How much demand there was compared with shares on offer. '25 times subscribed' means bids for 25 times the shares available.
A company controlled by another (its parent), usually through owning more than half its shares.
When the price pushes past a recent swing high or swing low but cannot hold there and closes back inside the earlier range.
The short code a stock trades under, such as RELIANCE on the NSE, and the six-digit number BSE uses, such as 500325.
IPO shares must list within three working days after the issue closes (T). Allotment is finalised on T+1, shares are credited and unused money unblocked on T+2, and listing happens on T+3.
The price-to-earnings multiple you assume the shares will trade at at the end of a scenario, used to turn a projected EPS into a price.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Future EPS × Target P/E

terms.meaning: An amount you can subtract from income before tax is calculated, such as Section 80C investments under the old tax regime.
terms.formula: Taxable income = Gross income − Deductions

terms.meaning: Tax withheld by the payer, such as a company paying dividends or a bank paying interest, and paid to the government on your behalf.
Studying price and trading volume to judge trends and momentum, rather than studying the business itself (fundamental analysis).

FinLit's two price-trend scores: a short-term view of recent weeks and a long-term view of the past year. Trend alignment puts the two together in plain words, such as 'Rising on both', 'Dip in an uptrend' or 'Falling on both'.
In a DCF, the value of all the cash flows after the forecast years, rolled into one figure at the end of the forecast.
terms.formula: Terminal value = Final-year FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)

terms.meaning: How long a price or NAV stayed below its previous high before getting back to it, or how long it has been below it so far.
The full gain from an investment: price change plus dividends or interest received.
terms.formula: Total return % = (End value − Start value + Income) ÷ Start value × 100

terms.meaning: How far an index fund or ETF's returns drift from the returns of the index it follows, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
terms.formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (fund return − index return)
aliases: Tracking error against the price index

terms.meaning: Volume multiplied by price: the rupee value of shares traded in a day.

An exchange segment where every trade must be settled by delivery, so shares bought cannot be sold the same day. Stocks under surveillance or with other concerns are moved into it, marked on NSE by series such as BE.

terms.term: Trading charges (brokerage, STT, stamp duty and others)
terms.meaning: The costs of a trade on top of the price: brokerage, securities transaction tax (STT), exchange transaction charges, the SEBI turnover fee, stamp duty, GST on brokerage and charges, and DP charges when shares leave your demat account.
One trading day on the exchange. NSE and BSE equity trading runs from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST on weekdays, after a pre-open session from 9:00 am.
How much a fund's NAV changed from a date in the past (one month, six months, one year...) up to the latest NAV.
terms.formula:
1-year return = (Latest NAV ÷ NAV one year earlier) − 1
For more than a year: (Latest NAV ÷ Start NAV)^(365 ÷ days between the two NAV dates) − 1

terms.meaning: A short-term Government of India security (91, 182 or 364 days) issued at a discount and repaid at face value.
The general direction of prices over time: up, down or sideways.
A straight line drawn on a price chart through two or more highs or lows to mark the direction of a trend.
The total of the last four reported quarters, used instead of the last full fiscal year.
A promise, usually by banks, to buy shares that investors do not take up, so the company raises the planned amount. More broadly, judging and taking on a risk, as in loans or insurance.
The share of people in the labour force who are looking for work but do not have it. In India it comes from MoSPI's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
terms.formula: Unemployment rate = Unemployed ÷ Labour force × 100

terms.meaning: The paper profit or loss on an investment you still hold.
terms.formula: Unrealised gain = Current market value − Purchase cost

terms.meaning: A loan with no collateral, such as a personal loan or credit card, given on the basis of your credit history.
The approval request you accept in your UPI app to block IPO money, used for applications up to ₹5 lakh.
Working out what an asset or company is worth, and comparing that with its price.
terms.formula: DCF value = Sum of FCF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t

terms.meaning: Style buckets for stocks: value stocks trade at low valuations, growth stocks at high valuations backed by fast growth, and blend sits in between.
A cost that rises and falls with how much is produced or sold, such as raw materials or delivery charges.
terms.formula: Total cost = Fixed cost + (Variable cost per unit × Units)

terms.meaning: Money invested in young, fast-growing private companies in exchange for a share of ownership.
How much a price swings up and down, usually measured as the standard deviation of returns and stated per year.
terms.formula: Volatility = Standard deviation of returns

terms.meaning: A stretch when a share's daily price range narrows well below its usual width. A breakout from a squeeze is the first strong move out of the narrow range.
The number of shares traded in a period, usually a day.

terms.term: Volume profile (value area and point of control)
terms.meaning: A count of how much volume traded at each price over a period. The point of control is the price with the most volume; the value area is the band around it where most of the volume, usually about 70%, traded.
The blended yearly cost of a company's funding: the return shareholders expect plus the after-tax interest on its debt, weighted by how much of each it uses.
terms.formula: WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − Tax rate)

terms.meaning: Your list of stocks to follow, with notes and price targets.
The average number of shares outstanding during a period, with each share counted for the part of the period it existed.
terms.formula: Weighted average shares = Σ (shares outstanding × fraction of the period outstanding)

terms.meaning: The share of closed trades that ended in a profit.
terms.formula: Win rate % = Winning trades ÷ All closed trades × 100

terms.meaning: The money tied up in day-to-day operations: short-term assets (cash, inventory, receivables) minus short-term liabilities (payables, short-term debt).
terms.formula: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

terms.meaning: eXtensible Business Reporting Language: a standard format for tagging financial statements so computers can read them.
The annualised return for investments made on different dates, such as monthly SIPs.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_i ÷ (1 + XIRR)^((d_i − d_0) ÷ 365)

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the same period a year earlier, such as Jun 2026 quarter against Jun 2025 quarter.
terms.formula: YoY % = (This period − Same period last year) ÷ Same period last year × 100
aliases: Operating profit growth, year on year
Profit growth vs same quarter last year
Sales growth vs same quarter last year

terms.meaning: The income an investment pays each year as a percentage of its price.
terms.formula: Current yield = Yearly income ÷ Current price

terms.meaning: The total yearly return you would earn on a bond if you hold it until maturity and every payment is made.
terms.formula: Price = Sum of C ÷ (1 + YTM)^t + Face value ÷ (1 + YTM)^n

terms.meaning: Building each budget from zero, justifying every expense, instead of starting from last year's figures.
A bond that pays no regular interest. It is sold below face value and repays face value at maturity; the difference is your return.
terms.formula: Price = Face value ÷ (1 + r)^n
